absent: Allocation, reservation, and commit protocol for the printk ringbuffer beyond block sizing and wrap detection.
Descriptor state machine and reader synchronization for printk records.
Console registration, flag management, and usability determination.
Nonblocking context acquisition, release, and takeover priority rules beyond single-record outcome.
Full panic entry sequence, notifier ordering, and kexec interaction beyond SMP coordination shown.
Device guard implementation and interrupt-safe printk region semantics.
Log formatting, extended versus standard layout, and message retrieval details.
Timing suppression and dependency annotation semantics.
Backtrace triggering implementation and processor selection.
Timeout and progress-reset behavior of the timed flushing implementation.

findings.text: Data block reservation size accounts for a header footprint added to payload length and then rounds upward to the alignment required by the block identifier.

Ring generation is derived by shifting a logical position by a configured width; wrapping for a candidate extent compares generations at its start and at its inclusive end so exactly fitting extents do not count as wrapped.
Line tally over bounded text starts at one and adds one per newline byte found by bounded search until exhaustion or absence of further newlines.
Oldest readable sequence is either a constant denoting absence of buffering in one build or the sequence discovered by a validity probe that yields zero when nothing is readable.

Single-record flushing skips consoles able to advance through alternate paths, considers only currently usable consoles, advances each eligible console by at most one record, reports whether any console qualified, tracks the greatest flushed sequence seen, signals repetition when advancement occurred, propagates handover, and abandons work when a foreign panic owner appears.

Outer flushing initializes sequence and handover reporting and repeats single passes while advancement is signalled; the locked region additionally rechecks readability of the successor sequence after release to determine whether another acquisition is justified.

Legacy emission looks up the successor of a console position, accumulates loss counts, advances past empty formatted results without hardware action, surfaces loss indication for non-extended output, and either writes directly in forced threaded builds or through a protected hardware section otherwise; an alternate build always reports absence of work.
Selection between direct threaded writes and protected hardware writes is governed by a build-chosen constant that holds uniformly true in one configuration and uniformly false in another.

Rewind moves every console position to the oldest currently readable sequence, using a nonblocking install for one console family and direct assignment for the other; the install raises requested values to the oldest readable position to accommodate truncated sequence storage, while an alternate header form is a neutral no-op.

Nonblocking legacy emission binds a write context to a console with default priority and delegates to a single-record emitter; the emitter holds backing context only across one record attempt, treats handover or takeover as loss of responsibility, releases on success, and reports backlog presence as progress; header fallbacks for sequence query and legacy emission provide neutral zero and absence values.
Interrupt-guarded printk regions either combine masking with explicit safe-region bracketing or reduce to masking alone, depending on build selection.
Permission for spinlock use across legacy hardware writes is either empty or a balanced attempt and release pair surrounding the device call.

Forced panic relocation requires enabled configuration, distinct local and destination processors, online destination, absence of concurrent panic, and success in single-winner claiming; eligible attempts prepare a message with static fallback, raise verbosity, emit conditional diagnostics, and dispatch an interprocessor request whose failure releases the claim and resumes local handling, while an alternate build always declines.

Panic shutdown of peer processors optionally produces backtraces under a temporary permission window that omits the already-reported local processor when appropriate, then chooses standard stop versus crash-oriented stop from dump intent; crash-oriented stop takes effect at most once.

Verbosity activation raises the console threshold to its most permissive level unless disabled or already silent; generic timed flushing delegates to a shared routine with timeout and progress-reset policy while one build always reports success; panic synchronization enabling records permission and nudges the console lock when direct legacy flushing is active; unsafe atomic flushing brackets pending-sequence draining with temporary takeover permission.

Two globally visible operations bracket spinning ownership around emission: one records the current holder with waiting annotation, the other clears ownership, wakes any waiter, preserves unlock ordering, and reports handover occurrence, with annotation-only behavior while panic is active.

Globally visible console synchronization offers sleeping acquisition that waits out foreign panic ownership, nonblocking acquisition that fails under the same condition, and release that flushes when direct legacy output is active and otherwise only releases.

Nonblocking console facilities visible across files provide legacy single-record emission with handover reporting, forced sequence installation clamped to availability, and panic-time unsafe draining of pending work.

Panic coordination exposes a never-returning local stop, a default redirection built on an asynchronous single-target request, a single-winner start claim, a once-only crash stop, and a taint flag query.

Kernel services expose verbosity control, panic synchronization enabling, display unblanking over usable consoles, timed log flushing, and oldest-readable sequence query with a constant fallback in one build.

Console list traversal for flushing, rewinding, and unblanking holds a read-side guard across the walk; handover paths drop that guard before transferring counting-lock ownership to preserve ordering, and foreign panic ownership aborts iteration.

Spinning ownership uses a dedicated raw guard protecting holder identity in console_owner and waiter presence in console_waiter with single-copy access; wake clears waiter presence under the guard and passes counting-lock ownership onward, while panic execution skips holder tracking.

Non-atomic nonblocking emission serializes on the device guard with migration disabled, while atomic emission uses an interrupt-masked safe region with spinning enabled and timing suppressed; backing context is retained only for the single-record attempt.

Counting-lock acquisition marks the subsystem locked and records scheduling permissibility, allowing scheduling for sleeping acquisition and forbidding it for nonblocking attempts; release clears the locked mark, with semaphore helpers coupling counting operations to dependency annotations.

Unblanking probes for interested consoles without exclusivity, then takes exclusivity with best-effort attempt under fault context and sleeping acquisition otherwise while skipping nonmaskable context entirely, holding the locked mark across hardware callbacks before release; legacy device writes run masked with timing suppressed and optional spinlock permission.

Observed state comprises a data ring width in size_bits governing generation, a data block identifier governing alignment, a console with sequence in seq and loss in dropped plus write and unblank callbacks, a flush selector with atomic and offload and direct modes, a message view with buffer set and length and loss and sequence, and a write context binding console with priority and backlog.

Flushing terminates on quiescence, handover, foreign panic ownership, or inability to advance usable consoles; otherwise per-console advancement compels another pass and post-release discovery of new readable work compels reacquisition.

Eligible relocation claims single-winner ownership, prepares messaging, dispatches transfer, and ends in local stop after successful dispatch or in claim release with local continuation after dispatch failure.
Unblanking progresses through capability probing, conditional acquisition, guarded iteration with hardware invocation, release, and timed flushing outside fault context.
Panic multiprocessor handling is entered via single-winner start claim, default redirection request, and never-returning local stop after successful redirection.
Console service entry includes verbosity raising, panic synchronization enabling, display unblanking, timed flushing, and unsafe atomic draining for panic-time output.
Nonblocking output and ringbuffer inspection are entered through legacy emission, forced sequence installation, and oldest-readable query with constant fallback in one build.
Once handover is signalled the read-side guard is already released and prior console references are invalid; callers abandon further passes and report lack of success.

While panic is active, waiting spinners receive no service, acquisition defers to a foreign panic owner, legacy rewinding proceeds only on best effort without exclusivity, and unblanking avoids counting-lock use inside nonmaskable context while tolerating possibly halted holders elsewhere.

Narrow retained sequence suffixes require clamping of rewind and force targets to currently readable positions; loss tallies persist across skips and surface on later output, while empty formatted results advance position without device action.
